comment: 1. **[Major]** The manuscript's clearest empirical result, that anorthite dissolution and calcite dissolution are exactly indistinguishable under an 11-ion panel because "both reactions were written to load identically onto calcium and bicarbonate" (lines 479-483), is presented as though newly exposed by the null-space diagnostic. It is not a new observation in geochemistry. Congruent silicate weathering of plagioclase to kaolinite and calcite dissolution both release calcium and bicarbonate in a 1:2 molar ratio, which is precisely why the field has spent several decades building independent tracers, most prominently 87Sr/86Sr, to separate carbonate from silicate weathering sources when major-ion stoichiometry alone cannot (see, for example, the body of work reviewed in strontium-isotope weathering-discrimination studies going back to the 1990s). The Introduction cites Christophersen and Hooper (1992) for the general equifinality point in end-member mixing but does not connect the anorthite/calcite finding to this specific, well-established literature, which means the manuscript's most quotable result reads as more novel than it is and misses an opportunity to point readers toward the actual solution the field already uses (Sr or other isotope tracers) rather than only naming an entropy-based evidence index. Add a paragraph in the Introduction or Discussion citing the silicate-versus-carbonate weathering discrimination literature and explicitly stating that Sr-isotope or similar independent tracers are the established remedy for exactly this ambiguity, which the ELRI enhanced-tier diagnostics in this study only partially reproduce.
requested_action: Address the finding in full while preserving the manuscript's evidence boundary.

comment: 2. **[Major]** The literature review does not engage with any 2023-2025 work. Every citation on inverse hydrogeochemical or mixing methodology (Christophersen and Hooper 1992, Plummer and Back 1980, Plummer et al. 1994, Beven and Freer 2001, Beven 2006, Neuman 2003, Tibshirani 1996, Zou and Hastie 2005, Meinshausen and Bühlmann 2010) predates 2020, and the one genuinely recent citation, Moracchini et al. (2025) on graph-based contaminant transport, is explicitly framed as adjacent rather than on-topic ("developed independently for transport-scenario screening rather than for chemistry," lines 69-71). A search for recent inverse geochemical modelling work turns up active 2023-2025 publications combining multivariate statistics with inverse geochemical modelling in shallow groundwater, and a growing body of physics-informed neural network work applied to reactive transport and inverse hydrogeochemical problems, none of which is mentioned. Given the field-transfer component uses Northern Ghana data collected in 2025, this also means no post-2011 regional geochemistry literature on Ghanaian basement aquifers is cited even though nearly fifteen years have passed. Add at least two to three citations from 2022-2025 covering either machine-learning approaches to inverse geochemical or reactive-transport inference, or updated regional Ghana groundwater geochemistry, and state explicitly how this study's approach differs from them.

comment: 1. **[Major]** The Mechanism Resolution Score's headline transfer statistic is benchmarked against the wrong baseline. The manuscript reports "48.9% four-class classification accuracy on the untouched mixed archetype... materially better than the 25% expected under random four-class assignment" (lines 506-509, repeated in the Abstract and Conclusion). I recomputed the true-class distribution directly from `results/mechanism_resolution_scores.csv` on the exact 900-row held-out evaluation set used to generate this statistic (archetype == "mixed"): non_identifiable 334 rows (37.1%), partially_identifiable 338 rows (37.6%), identifiable 206 rows (22.9%), equivalence_class 22 rows (2.4%). A trivial "always predict partially_identifiable" rule would score 37.6% on this exact evaluation set, not 25%. I independently recomputed the reported accuracy from the same file's `resolution_class_correct` column (440/900 = 48.89%), confirming the 48.9% figure itself is genuine and traceable, so this is not a fabrication concern. But comparing it only to a uniform-random baseline overstates the realised skill: the margin over a naive majority-class rule is roughly 11.3 percentage points, not the roughly 24-point margin implied by comparing to 25%. This matters because the MRS is one of the five headline innovations claimed in the Introduction, and the manuscript already hedges "48.9% is a moderate, not a strong, transfer result" (lines 511-512), which is the right instinct but is undercut by anchoring the comparison to the easier baseline throughout. Report the majority-class baseline (37.6%) alongside the uniform-random baseline in Methods (Supplementary Methods S4), Results, and Discussion, and revise the "materially better than... random" language to state the margin over both baselines.
requested_action: Address the finding in full while preserving the manuscript's evidence boundary.

comment: 2. **[Major]** Bounded least squares, the only unregularised comparator, converged in only 35.4% of fits (Table 1), yet its reported phase F1 (0.435) and false-discovery rate (0.697) are computed by "retaining and flagging" non-convergent fits rather than reporting them separately (lines 419-423, "Non-convergent fits were retained and flagged rather than discarded, so all reported recovery statistics reflect the full factorial design"). This is defensible as a design choice for avoiding convergence-filtered survivorship bias, but it also means bounded least squares' comparator statistics conflate "the optimiser did not converge" with "the optimiser converged and selected the wrong reaction," and these are different failure modes with different implications for the paper's central message about sparsity versus thermodynamic guarding. Since the point of this comparator is to isolate the effect of sparsity regularisation, and 64.6% of its fits never reached the solver's own stopping criterion, the headline comparison between bounded least squares and the guarded model is partly a comparison between a poorly-converging optimiser and a well-converging one, not purely between an unregularised and a regularised objective. Report phase F1 and false-discovery rate for bounded least squares separately for converged and non-converged subsets, or at minimum note in the main text how much of the reported gap narrows when restricted to converged fits only.
requested_action: Address the finding in full while preserving the manuscript's evidence boundary.

comment: 3. **[Major]** Two of the five headline innovations, held-out-ion falsification and next-best-measurement selection, are supported in the main text only by references to Supplementary Figures S8 and S9, with no inline effect size, confidence interval, or quantitative comparator value anywhere in the "Missing ions and minimum analytical information" subsection (lines 516-531). comment: 3. **[Major]** The Discussion's "Advance over existing inverse hydrogeochemical practice" section states that the framework's components are "pre-existing statistical tools... combined into a reaction-inference identifiability layer" (lines 708-710), which is an honest and appropriate framing, but the same section's conceptual-advance claim, "a shift from exact-phase selection to hierarchical reporting across four resolution classes... each backed by an explicit diagnostic rather than an implicit confidence claim" (lines 720-724), is not tested against any competing reporting convention beyond the conventional PHREEQC first-minimal-model baseline built by the same authors for this study.
